name: Kidneys
func: Filter the blood to remove waste and extra water as urine. They also keep salt, potassium, acid and blood pressure in balance and make hormones that build red blood cells and activate vitamin D.

levels.kid:
You have two **kidneys**, and each one is shaped like a big bean about the size of your fist. They sit in your back, just under your lowest ribs, one on each side.

Your kidneys are like a super-smart cleaning machine for your blood. All day long, blood flows through them. They keep the good stuff your body needs, and they pull out the trash and extra water. That trash and water become **pee** (urine).

The pee slides down two thin tubes into a stretchy bag called your bladder, and then you go to the bathroom.

Drinking water helps your kidneys do their job. They work every single minute, even while you sleep!
levels.hs:
The **kidneys** are two bean-shaped organs about 11 cm long, lying against the back wall of the abdomen on either side of the spine, roughly from the T12 to L3 vertebrae. They are **retroperitoneal**, meaning they sit behind the lining of the abdominal cavity. The right kidney sits a little lower than the left because the liver is above it. An **adrenal gland** caps the top of each kidney.

Each kidney has an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla** arranged into cone-shaped **pyramids**. Urine drains from the pyramids into cup-like **calyces**, then the **renal pelvis**, then the ureter.

The working unit is the **nephron**, and each kidney has around a million of them. A nephron has a filter (the **glomerulus**) and a long tube that reabsorbs what the body needs (water, glucose, salt) and secretes what it doesn't. Together the kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid a day but make only about 1.5 litres of urine.

The kidneys also control blood pressure, balance potassium and acid, release **erythropoietin** (EPO) to make red blood cells, and activate vitamin D.
levels.college:
Each kidney lies in the **paravertebral gutter** on the posterior abdominal wall, resting on the psoas major, quadratus lumborum and diaphragm, wrapped in **perirenal fat** and **renal (Gerota's) fascia**. The 12th rib crosses the back of both kidneys, and the 11th crosses the left. Anteriorly the right kidney touches the liver, duodenum and hepatic flexure of the colon; the left touches the stomach, spleen, pancreas tail, jejunum and descending colon.

At the **hilum** the structures run, from front to back, **renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis** ("VAP"). The kidneys receive about **20–25% of cardiac output**.

The **nephron** sequence: glomerulus in Bowman's capsule → **proximal convoluted tubule** (reabsorbs ~65% of filtered sodium and water, all glucose and amino acids) → **loop of Henle** (builds the medullary concentration gradient by countercurrent multiplication) → **distal convoluted tubule** → **collecting duct**, where **ADH** inserts aquaporin-2 channels to concentrate urine and **aldosterone** drives sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

**Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** is the key measure of kidney function, normally around 90–120 mL/min/1.73 m². The **renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system** starts at the kidney's **juxtaglomerular apparatus**, linking the kidney directly to blood pressure control.
levels.phd:
The **glomerular filtration barrier** has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, the **glomerular basement membrane** (type IV collagen α3/α4/α5 network), and **podocyte** foot processes joined by **slit diaphragms** built from **nephrin** and **podocin**. Mutations in NPHS1 (nephrin) cause congenital nephrotic syndrome; COL4A3–5 mutations cause **Alport syndrome**. The barrier selects by size and charge, so albumin is normally almost completely excluded.

Tubular transport is organised around the basolateral **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase**. Apical carriers differ by segment: **NHE3** and SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, **NKCC2** in the thick ascending limb, **NCC** in the distal convoluted tubule, and **ENaC** in principal cells of the collecting duct. These are the exact targets of loop diuretics, thiazides, SGLT2 inhibitors and potassium-sparing drugs, and inherited loss of them gives Bartter and Gitelman syndromes.

**Tubuloglomerular feedback**: **macula densa** cells sense chloride delivery and adjust afferent arteriole tone (via adenosine) and renin release, autoregulating GFR. Together with the myogenic response, this keeps GFR stable across a wide range of blood pressures.

Urine concentration depends on the countercurrent loop plus **urea recycling** via UT-A transporters and the **vasa recta**, which act as countercurrent exchangers. **Peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells** sense hypoxia through **HIF-2α** and secrete erythropoietin; failing kidneys therefore cause anaemia. Proximal tubule cells express **1α-hydroxylase**, making active calcitriol. Active research areas include kidney organoids, single-cell atlases of nephron segments, and why SGLT2 inhibition slows chronic kidney disease.
levels.expert:
Clinically, kidney function is tracked by **serum creatinine**, **eGFR**, electrolytes (normal potassium about 3.5–5.0 mmol/L) and urinalysis. **Acute kidney injury** is classified as **prerenal** (low perfusion, e.g. dehydration or shock), **intrinsic** (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis) or **postrenal** (obstruction). **Nephrotic syndrome** shows heavy proteinuria, low albumin and oedema; **nephritic syndrome** shows blood in the urine, red-cell casts, hypertension and reduced GFR.

On exam, the kidneys are rarely palpable except when enlarged (e.g. **polycystic kidney disease**, which also links to intracranial **berry aneurysms**, a neurosurgical overlap). **Costovertebral angle tenderness** suggests pyelonephritis. A classic **renal colic** from a stone radiates from loin to groin.

**Imaging**: ultrasound is first-line for size, hydronephrosis and cysts; non-contrast **CT KUB** is the standard for stones; contrast CT stages renal masses (renal cell carcinoma can extend into the renal vein and IVC). Iodinated contrast and some drugs are nephrotoxic, so eGFR is checked before scans.

**Surgery**: partial or radical nephrectomy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy through the flank, and **kidney transplantation**, where the donor kidney is placed in the iliac fossa and joined to the external iliac vessels. Surgeons respect the **pleura** (the 12th rib approach risks pneumothorax) and the duodenum and IVC near the right hilum.

End-stage disease is managed with dialysis or transplant; general treatment of chronic kidney disease includes blood pressure control and RAAS blockade.

keyPoints: Retroperitoneal, T12–L3; right kidney sits lower because of the liver
Hilum order front to back: vein, artery, pelvis
Nephron = glomerulus + tubule; ~1 million per kidney
Filters ~180 L/day, makes ~1.5 L of urine
Also makes EPO and active vitamin D and controls blood pressure via renin

test.q: Which kidney usually sits lower, and why?
choices: They are always at the same level
test.explain: The large liver pushes the right kidney slightly downward.

test.q: The filtering tuft of capillaries in each nephron is the ______.
test.explain: The glomerulus sits inside Bowman's capsule and filters plasma.

test.q: Which hormone made by the kidney stimulates red blood cell production?
test.explain: Interstitial cells sense low oxygen and secrete erythropoietin (EPO).

test.q: At the renal hilum, what is the most anterior structure?
test.explain: Front to back: vein, artery, pelvis.

test.q: Which hormone inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct to concentrate urine?
test.explain: ADH (vasopressin) makes the collecting duct permeable to water.
